name: Spinal segment C1
function: The C1 segment of the spinal cord contains the sensory interneurons and motor neurons whose rootlets form the C1 nerve root. Its cutaneous field is the C1 dermatome (none — the C1 nerve has no cutaneous distribution), and its ventral horn motor neurons supply the suboccipital muscles (rectus capitis posterior major and minor, obliquus capitis superior and inferior). The dorsal rootlets deliver primary afferents to the dorsal horn and the ventral rootlets carry motor axons out through the intervertebral foramen; the roots of this segment exit near the correspondingly numbered vertebra.

afferent: Primary afferents of the C1 dorsal rootlets (tract-dorsal-rootlets)
efferent: Motor axons of the C1 ventral rootlets (tract-ventral-rootlets)

bloodSupply: Anterior spinal artery (vasc-anterior-spinal-artery-cord) through sulcocommissural branches, reinforced at the dorsal root entry zone by the posterior spinal arteries (vasc-posterior-spinal-arteries).

clinical.syndrome: C1 radiculopathy or segmental cord injury
clinical.findings: Motor involvement produces weakness of the suboccipital muscles (rectus capitis posterior major and minor, obliquus capitis superior and inferior); sensory involvement produces numbness or neuropathic pain of none — the C1 nerve has no cutaneous distribution, with loss of the segmental reflex arc. The root is essentially motor; isolated injury produces suboccipital weakness and neck pain without a dermatome.

name: Spinal cord (context envelope)
synonyms: neuraxis caudal to the cervicomedullary junction
function: The context envelope of the spinal cord: the caudal continuation of the neuraxis from the cervicomedullary junction at the foramen magnum to the conus medullaris. It contains the H-shaped central gray matter surrounded by the three funiculi of white matter, the central canal, and the segmental root entry and exit zones. Thirty-one spinal segments from C1 to Co1 are addressed through the shared level-addressing contract, and the cervical and lumbar enlargements mark the limb plexuses. Only cord segments are modeled here, not the vertebral column, so segment-to-vertebra relationships are described in the records but not drawn.

afferent: Dorsal rootlets (tract-dorsal-rootlets) at every segment
efferent: Ventral rootlets (tract-ventral-rootlets) at every segment

bloodSupply: Anterior spinal artery (vasc-anterior-spinal-artery-cord) and posterior spinal arteries (vasc-posterior-spinal-arteries).

clinical.syndrome: Complete cord transection (trauma, transverse myelitis)
clinical.findings: Bilateral motor, sensory and autonomic loss below the lesion with spinal shock initially, followed by spasticity and a reflex bladder; any sacral sparing indicates an incomplete lesion and changes the prognosis.

name: Conus medullaris
function: The tapered caudal end of the spinal cord, containing the sacral and coccygeal segments and ending at the filum terminale. It houses the sacral parasympathetic nucleus and the motor neurons of the bladder and anal sphincters, so conus lesions produce early sphincter dysfunction. In adults it lies near the L1-L2 vertebral level.

afferent: Sacral afferents from the perineum and pelvic viscera entering through the dorsal rootlets (tract-dorsal-rootlets)
efferent: Sacral parasympathetic and somatic motor axons leaving through the ventral rootlets (tract-ventral-rootlets)

clinical.syndrome: Conus medullaris syndrome
clinical.findings: Early sphincter dysfunction with saddle anaesthesia, symmetric bilateral leg weakness and an absent bulbocavernosus reflex; onset is abrupt and pain is less prominent than in cauda equina syndrome.

name: Filum terminale
function: The slender glial thread that extends from the tip of the conus medullaris through the lumbar cistern to attach to the coccyx, anchoring the caudal end of the cord. It is a vestige of the embryonic spinal cord and is surrounded by the roots of the cauda equina within the dural sac.

afferent: No neural input; the filum is a connective tissue extension of the pia mater
efferent: No neural output

bloodSupply: Small filial branches of the segmental arteries (vasc-anterior-radiculomedullary-arteries).

clinical.syndrome: Tethered cord (thickened filum terminale)
clinical.findings: Mechanical traction on the conus during growth causes progressive gait disturbance, bladder dysfunction, scoliosis and foot deformity with a low-lying conus on imaging.

spinalSpan.basis: The filum descends from the conus past the coccygeal segment to the sacral attachment; the modeled extent stops at the CLIP_BOUNDS floor (y = -390) while the level addressing keeps its Co1 anchor.
